web_title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk
book_title: Chapter 5: The Operating Dashboard, Capacity Roadmap & CEO Walk-the-Talk
question: Which 5–6 leading operational KPIs govern Macpower's trajectory over the next three years, and has management delivered on its prior commitments?

epigraph.quote: Do not listen to what management hopes for in year five; measure what they built in year one against what they promised last year.
epigraph.author: Forensic Governance Standard

web_blocks.html: CNC machine tools are long-lead capital goods, so reported quarterly revenue is a lagging indicator. Analysts must track six leading KPIs to read Macpower's structural health ahead of the P&L [4, 15, 16]. These cover (1) Pending Order Book and Advance-Backed Coverage, (2) NEXA Premium Mix Share, and (3) Capacity Utilization and Expansion Milestones. They also include (4) Average Realization per Machine, (5) Government and Defence Tender Pipeline Conversion, and (6) Working Capital and Inventory Days [4, 15, 16].

web_blocks.takeaway: Demand KPIs (₹476.7 Cr order book, 40% NEXA mix, ₹20.36L realization) are firing on all cylinders, but physical capacity (95% full, refunding 10–20 orders/month) and a shrinking government tender pipeline (₹1,942M) require close monitoring [15].

web_blocks.html: Management's expansion plan is sequenced across two distinct land parcels. In July 2026, Macpower leased 13 acres (~9 acres buildable) near Metoda for 30 years [6, 15]. The company will build a 150,000–200,000 sq ft centrally air-conditioned assembly plant there at an estimated ₹50 Cr cost [6, 15]. Under the Viksit Gujarat Industrial Policy 2026, this project qualifies for up to a 25% capital subsidy and a 7% interest subsidy [6, 15]. That support cuts effective bank borrowing costs from ~8.25% to ~1.25% [6, 15]. Civil work and 20% of long-lead machinery orders (spindle, sheet-metal, and telescopic covers) are already underway [15]. Commissioning is targeted by the end of Q2 FY28 [15]. A second, larger 60-acre Gujarat government parcel is planned for a ₹100 Cr Phase-1 defence and backward-integration hub [6, 7, 15]. That hub aims to lift component self-sufficiency toward 75%–80% [6, 7, 15]. More than 32+ departmental clearances are complete and token money is paid, but handover remains stalled awaiting the state's revised defence and aerospace policy [6, 7, 15].

web_blocks.takeaway: Management has a strong execution record on factory additions, margin expansion, and cash collection—the areas within its direct control—while government-dependent timelines (60-acre land) have slipped repeatedly [15].

web_blocks.html: For FY27, management guides for ~35% revenue growth, implying ~₹450 Cr in sales [4, 15]. Over the following three years (FY27–FY29), it targets 25%–30% annual growth [4, 15]. That target depends on commissioning the 13-acre assembly plant by Q2 FY28 and lifting NEXA's order-book share from 40% toward 50% [4, 15]. To support that scale, Macpower is doubling its sales and service team by FY27-end [15]. It also plans to add ~2,000 staff over the next 2–3 years, so fixed payroll costs will rise ahead of new-plant revenue [15]. Management's long-term >20% EBITDA margin goal still depends on the delayed 60-acre backward-integration plant rather than near-term operating leverage alone [6, 7, 15].

book_paragraphs: If you only read Macpower's quarterly profit-and-loss statement, you are driving by looking in the rearview mirror. By the time a ₹2 crore Double Column Machine is invoiced, the customer placed the order six months earlier. That is why you and I need a six-point leading dashboard to see around corners. First is the pending order book, which reached ₹476.7 crore in September 2026—up 36% in a year, 2.7 times higher than three years ago, and equal to four full quarters of Q2 FY27 output. Even better, every non-dealer, non-government order in that book is backed by a customer cash advance. Second is the NEXA share inside that backlog, which climbed from 28% in March 2025 to 40% in September 2026, pulling average machine realization up from ₹18.48 lakh to ₹20.36 lakh.

Third—and most urgent—is physical plant utilization. At 591 machines in Q2 FY27 against a quarterly capacity of 625 machines, the Metoda plant is running at 95% capacity. Rupesh Mehta admitted in October 2026 that Macpower is actually refunding customer advances on 10 to 20 machines every month simply because it has run out of assembly floor space. That is a high-class problem to have, but every refunded deposit is a customer walking across the street to Jyoti CNC or Ace Micromatic. Until the new 13-acre air-conditioned assembly plant—a ₹50 crore investment backed by a 25% capital subsidy and 7% interest subsidy under the Viksit Gujarat Industrial Policy, cutting net borrowing cost to roughly 1.25%—comes online by Q2 FY28, growth will be capped by square footage, not demand.

Fourth and fifth are the two yellow flags on our dashboard: the government tender pipeline under evaluation dropped from ₹3,760 million in March 2026 to ₹1,942 million in September 2026 without a full reconciliation of wins versus lapses, and component bottlenecks in in-house spindles (currently 1,700–1,800 units/year) and sheet metal must be expanded alongside the new shed. Sixth is working capital days, which improved from 138 days in September 2025 to 110 days in September 2026.

To understand the multi-year structural potential, look at how management has sequenced its growth: ₹450 crore implied for FY27 (+35% growth), followed by 25% to 30% annual growth visibility over the next three years once the 13-acre plant relieves assembly bottlenecks. At the same time, management is doubling its sales and service team by the end of FY27 and plans to add roughly 2,000 employees over two to three years. That means you should expect staff and branch costs to rise ahead of revenue, keeping near-term EBITDA margins near 16% to 17% rather than jumping to 20%+ until the 60-acre backward-integration plant is eventually built.

Now let us run a Walk-the-Talk audit on Rupesh Mehta. Over the past three years, what he promised inside his own factory gates, he delivered. He promised a 500-machine expansion in September 2024 and commissioned it on November 10, 2025. He promised 16% to 18% operating margins through backward integration and NEXA, and delivered 16.2% in FY26 and 16.6% in Q2 FY27. He raised FY27 revenue guidance twice—from 28% to 35%—and backed it up with 40.4% Q2 growth and ₹29.97 crore of operating cash flow in the first half.

Where has the record been mixed? Anywhere Macpower had to wait on government policy—most notably the 60-acre defence land parcel, which has sat in limbo for over a year waiting for Gujarat's revised defence policy—and in Q1 FY26, when an analyst caught a discrepancy between management's claimed order-inflow growth and the underlying quarterly run-rate. That honest scorecard tells us to trust Mehta's shop-floor execution, while discounting any timeline that depends on state bureaucracy.

book_callouts.title: RUPESH MEHTA, CMD (OCTOBER 2026)
book_callouts.quote: Our struggle with the customer is about deliveries.
book_callouts.text: When a machine-tool maker is refunding advances on 10 to 20 machines a month, demand is not the bottleneck—execution of the 13-acre plant by Q2 FY28 is the entire ballgame.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A Walk-the-Talk audit separates controllable execution from external promises. Macpower's management has earned high marks on factory debottlenecking, margin discipline, and receivables—while the 60-acre defence land remains a 'show-me' option rather than a base-case certainty.
